title: Influencer Marketing Campaigns: Types, Real Examples, and How to Measure Results
summary: Learn what influencer marketing campaigns are, compare the main campaign types, see real brand examples with results, and get a checklist to plan and measure your own.
body_markdown:
## Real Influencer Marketing Campaigns: Mini Case Studies With Named Metrics


Strong examples connect a business objective to a creator, a participation mechanic, and a measurable outcome. The cases below apply that logic to conversion, awareness, and retention. Not every public example includes a verified performance figure, so distinguish reported metrics from qualitative lessons.


### Conversion Play: Staples x Employee Creators and KFC x Co-Created Brand Identity


1.


**Staples Baddie:** The goal was to make a familiar retailer feel relevant through creator-led content. The account, associated with creator @blivxx, uses an employee persona and workplace humor to build a recognizable point of view. Those figures indicate audience response and distribution, but do not establish sales attribution. A mid-size brand can take away the value of a specific, repeatable creator concept rather than a generic product mention.


2.


**KFC co-created brand identity:** The campaign concept centered on bringing a creator’s perspective into brand identity work. That mechanic can invite audience participation and make creative choices more culturally relevant. The research supplied for this article does not include a verified result metric for this example, so no reach or sales figure is assigned. Define the business measure before launch, such as qualified visits, product interest, or sales, and report only results supported by campaign data.


### Awareness Play: DoorDash x Internet Fandoms and Strava x Local IRL Events


DoorDash’s internet-fandom approach uses familiar online communities and cultural references to make a brand message more shareable. Strava’s local event approach connects digital content with in-person participation, giving creators a reason to document an experience and audiences a clear way to join. One builds relevance through shared fandom; the other makes the brand visible through local activity.


The provided research does not verify named outcome metrics for these examples. Treat them as creative models, not proof of reach or lift. Choose the mechanic your audience already participates in, then track video views or event attendance alongside downstream signals such as branded searches or qualified site visits.


### Retention Play: Ambassador and Affiliate Rosters in DTC and NIL Programs


Recurring creator partnerships can support retention by keeping a product present across multiple customer touchpoints. OpenSponsorship reports that a sports nutrition roster of 12 athletes posting monthly for six months reduced cost per engagement by 40% compared with lifestyle creators and produced 72 reusable assets. These vendor-reported figures illustrate the value of audience fit and a planned cadence, not a guaranteed outcome for every brand.


For DTC and name, image, and likeness (NIL) programs, establish deliverables, posting frequency, usage terms, and a consistent way to track engagement or sales. A repeatable roster also creates a library of creator content to assess for future use, subject to agreed permissions.


### What Each Example Teaches a Mid-Size Brand


Build from the mechanic, not the headline. A creator-led persona needs a consistent voice; fandom content needs genuine cultural relevance; local events depend on accessible participation; and ambassador programs need a sustainable publishing cadence. Select creators for audience alignment and content fit, then set one primary objective before negotiating deliverables.


**Planning principle:** Separate attention metrics from business outcomes. Views and engagement show how people responded to content; tracked visits, orders, or repeat purchases provide a clearer connection to commercial performance. Label vendor-reported figures and do not present engagement as proof of sales.
